gist: David Roberts interviews Kristian Jensen, CEO of Green Power Denmark and former Danish finance minister, on why Denmark is off-track for its 70%-by-2030 target and how it plans to catch up: shifting from biomass and CCS bets toward direct electrification via district-heating heat pumps and thermal storage, EVs and V2G, a grid-priority law that puts data centers last, and Power-to-X exports to Germany.

themes.theme: Denmark's 70% target gap, CCS and peatlands

insights.claim: Denmark has cut emissions ~50% since 1990 but its legally binding 70%-by-2030 target looks off-track: the Independent Climate Council sees no government path and Concito's probabilistic modelling puts the odds of hitting it at about 1%.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Expect policy acceleration (gas phase-out, heat pumps, industrial electrification) to close the gap — a tailwind for Danish electrification suppliers.

insights.claim: Kristian Jensen argues the 2030 target is only reachable if policy changes — e.g. cutting gas pipelines to private homes and switching to heat pumps, plus more electrified industry — and that under frozen policy success would depend on luck with weather (wind/solar output, winter temperatures).
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Gas-grid disconnection mandates for households are a plausible next policy lever in Denmark; watch heat pump and gas distribution exposure.
insights.quote: It is out of reach if politicians don't do anything else.

insights.claim: Denmark's new coalition is proposing to raise its 2035 target to an 82%+ cut vs 1990, en route to climate neutrality by 2045, despite having already picked the low-hanging fruit.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Ratcheting targets imply harder, more intrusive measures on households and industry — more regulatory-driven demand for electrification equipment.

insights.claim: Jensen says energy-security shocks — the war in Ukraine and conflict around Hormuz — have made the cost of dependence on imported fossil fuels obvious and are the strongest political accelerant of Denmark's transition.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Geopolitical supply shocks reinforce European demand for domestic renewables and electrification regardless of climate politics.
insights.quote: in a very backward way they have been the biggest help we could could ask for.

insights.claim: Jensen believes the Danish government took a 'really, really big chance' on carbon capture and storage, spending a huge sum that could have bought more decarbonization elsewhere, chosen partly because it required little change from industry; most tendered projects have dropped out, leaving roughly one cement plant.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: CCS-dependent decarbonization pathways carry high delivery risk; capital may shift toward direct electrification and CCU/e-fuels.
insights.quote: they're taking a really, really big chance here.

insights.claim: Denmark recently began its first injection of CO2 into a depleted North Sea oil/gas field, with the Danish minister and the King pressing the start button.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: First operational North Sea storage is a milestone for Danish/European CO2 storage infrastructure players.

insights.claim: Taking peatlands and wetlands out of agricultural production is lagging — only about a third of where it was supposed to be by 2030 — because persuading farmers to leave land idle or swap land is complex.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Land-based sequestration under-delivers, pushing more of the burden onto the energy sector.

insights.claim: Denmark's share of electrified final energy has barely moved since 1990 despite a mostly renewable power mix; Jensen has described it as far along on renewable power but only ~2% of the way on the electrification needed, and says Danish electrification has been below the EU average.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: The next leg of the Danish transition is demand-side electrification (heat, transport, industry), not more generation alone.

insights.claim: Jensen attributes slow electrification to Denmark's heavy reliance on burning biomass (field straw, imported wood pellets) and biogas, plus high upfront costs of heat pumps despite low running costs.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Upfront-capex barriers suggest financing and grant schemes are the key unlocks for heat-pump adoption.

insights.claim: Jensen predicts the soon-to-be-published 2025 electrification-rate statistic will show a significant jump, driven by heat pumps and electric boilers in district heating since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: A data release to watch as confirmation of accelerating Danish electrification demand.

insights.claim: Green Power Denmark projects electricity production from biomass will fall to roughly one third of today's level over the next 10 years as wind and solar grow.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Negative long-term volume outlook for biomass/wood-pellet supply into Danish power generation.

insights.claim: Because Denmark is flat with essentially zero hydropower, Jensen argues biomass and biogas should be reserved as dispatchable backup for hours without wind and sun rather than used for baseload heat — 'much easier to save biogas than it is to save sunshine.'
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Biomass assets shift from baseload to peaking/backup roles — lower utilization but potentially higher capacity value.
insights.quote: it's much easier to save biogas than it is to save sunshine.

insights.claim: Jensen concedes Denmark's wood-pellet imports are 'not the finest moment' and says the country is tightening sustainability/certification standards on them.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Stricter sourcing rules plus declining biomass burn are headwinds for pellet exporters selling into Denmark.

themes.theme: Interconnectors, batteries and the data-center queue

insights.claim: Grid-scale and home battery penetration in Denmark is low because supply reliability is ~99.995% and Denmark leans on interconnectors to Sweden, Germany, the UK, Belgium and Norway as a two-way 'battery' — e.g. exporting surplus wind so Norway can save hydro water.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Interconnection substitutes for storage in Denmark; battery demand is only now emerging via price arbitrage.

insights.claim: Volatile hourly Danish power prices (cheap midday solar, expensive nights) are starting to make household battery arbitrage attractive, a recent trend.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Emerging residential storage market in Denmark driven by price spreads rather than backup.

insights.claim: Denmark has roughly 70 GW of grid-connection requests against a ~7 GW peak system, and Energinet imposed a moratorium on new connections; Jensen says most of that demand is speculative, with data centers applying at multiple sites they don't intend to use.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Headline data-center pipeline figures in Europe overstate real demand; discount connection-queue numbers.
insights.quote: The 70 gigawatts of demand that's out there is not real demand.

insights.claim: Jensen thinks a realistic Danish target is around 20–25 GW of connected demand ten years from now — a large but manageable increase versus today's ~7 GW peak.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Implies roughly a tripling of Danish load over a decade — significant grid, generation and transmission capex.

insights.claim: The Danish government is debating a grid-connection prioritization bill ranking health, defense and organic household growth (e.g. EVs) first; then industry, district heating, hydrogen and e-fuels; then batteries; and data centers last.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Data-center developers targeting Denmark face queue-priority risk; industrial and Power-to-X users get preferential grid access.

insights.claim: Many existing Danish data centers hold large connections they underuse (e.g. 1 GW contracted vs ~200 MW used), so data-center growth can continue even if new connections are deprioritized.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Existing connected data-center sites in Denmark gain scarcity value.

insights.claim: Jensen expects a new connection system allowing new grid customers to be added again within a few weeks, coordinated between local DSOs and TSO Energinet.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Watch for lifting of the Danish connection moratorium.

themes.theme: Municipal grid ownership and demand flexibility

insights.claim: Denmark's local distribution utilities are municipally/locally owned, revenue-capped non-profits whose strength is long-term investment horizons — e.g. many built fiber-optic broadband to every home, once derided as 'digging money into the ground', now a fantastic investment.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Patient-capital utility ownership enables infrastructure bets that quarterly-driven investors skip.

insights.claim: A weakness of the Danish local-utility model is that multi-billion companies are governed by lay boards, so boards increasingly add external specialists.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Governance professionalization is a theme for community-owned utilities.

insights.claim: A government mandate roughly 15 years ago put smart meters in Danish homes, and hourly pricing has significantly reduced morning and evening peak demand as consumers shift laundry and EV charging to cheap solar hours.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Dynamic pricing plus smart metering is a proven peak-shaving tool; supports flexibility and smart-home automation vendors.

insights.claim: Price-responsive smart appliances and heating controls are spreading rapidly in Denmark, but Jensen sees the bigger lever at industrial scale and in district heating.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Industrial and district-heating flexibility is the larger market than residential automation.

insights.claim: Jensen predicts thermal batteries — insulated hot-water storage charged with cheap power — will spread across Danish district heating systems in the coming years because they cut customer costs.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Growth market for thermal storage, electric boilers and large heat pumps in Nordic district heating.
insights.quote: thermal batteries right now are really going to spread all over Denmark in the coming years

themes.theme: Onshore wind and solar siting backlash

insights.claim: Danish onshore wind originally spread via 1970s–80s local co-ops with tax benefits; today environmental assessments and technical requirements make projects costlier and have pushed development to professional developers.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Permitting costs favor scale developers over community projects.

insights.claim: Solar farms in Denmark have grown very large because grid-connection and environmental-assessment costs are fixed regardless of size, and mandated green belts take time to grow — fueling backlash captured by a populist coinage that became Danish word of the year.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Regulatory fixed costs drive scale, which drives local opposition — a siting risk for European utility-scale solar.
insights.quote: the demands created by politician has actually pushed the solar farms to become larger.

insights.claim: Jensen expects large land-based solar farms to continue (splitting them up is uneconomic) alongside much more rooftop solar on municipal and industrial buildings.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Both rooftop C&I solar and utility-scale continue to grow in Denmark.

insights.claim: Selling a share of projects to locals (e.g. developer keeps four turbines, sells the fifth to residents) defuses opposition; Denmark's largest onshore turbine is owned by 2,800 local families and was built with zero complaints.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Community co-ownership structures materially de-risk permitting for renewables developers.
insights.quote: It is owned by 2,800 families in the municipality and it was created with zero complaints.

insights.claim: Danish agrivoltaics is shifting from sheep grazing toward shade-tolerant planted crops designed in from the start, and Jensen claims solar farms host more biodiversity than monocrop fields.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Agrivoltaics remains early-stage; acceptance rather than yield is the main value driver.

themes.theme: District heating's shift to heat pumps

insights.claim: About 70% of Danish households are on district heating, and replacing its biomass and gas will primarily use large heat pumps plus electric boilers, with geothermal only where geology allows (it works in Aarhus but a nearby attempt failed).
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Large-scale industrial heat pumps and e-boilers are the core capex category for Danish district heating.

insights.claim: Industrial heat pumps in district heating are already cheaper than gas or biogas without subsidies; the only constraint is access to credit, eased by municipal loan guarantees.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Unsubsidized economics make Danish district-heat electrification durable; financing, not policy, is the bottleneck.
insights.quote: the only thing holding them back right now is their access to credit.

insights.claim: The cheapest heat in Denmark comes from district heating plants that own their own wind or solar generation via a direct line feeding a large heat pump.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Co-located generation plus heat pumps is a model to watch for integrated heat-utility investment.

insights.claim: Denmark taxes fossil fuels, does not tax biomass, and gives state grants to rural households replacing oil or gas boilers with individual heat pumps; district heating gets no subsidy.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Residential heat-pump demand in rural Denmark is grant-supported; policy changes would affect installers.

insights.claim: Stranded-asset inertia slows the switch: district heating utilities that bought gas boilers ~6 years ago on 20-year paybacks resist early retirement without added incentives.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Turnover of energy capital stock is slow; expect gradual rather than abrupt heat-pump adoption absent retirement incentives.

insights.claim: Danish dairy cooperative Arla plans to convert all its dairy production sites to heat pumps, as a business case with returns comparable to its other investments rather than a policy requirement.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Industrial process-heat electrification is becoming economic in food processing — a demand signal for industrial heat-pump makers.

themes.theme: EV takeover, V2G and road pricing

insights.claim: Around 96% of new private car sales in Denmark are EVs (roughly 80–85% including fleets), initially driven by tax breaks but now sustained by price parity, lower running costs and a cultural shift.
insights.speaker: David Roberts (host)
insights.so_what: Denmark shows EV adoption can become self-sustaining once upfront price parity is reached; bearish for ICE resale values there.

insights.claim: Jensen says that even without the tax break, many EVs now have better lifetime total cost of ownership than combustion cars, and no one in Denmark wants to buy a used diesel or petrol car.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Residual-value risk for used ICE vehicles in high-EV markets.
insights.quote: No one will buy a used diesel or a petrol car in Denmark.

insights.claim: Dense charging infrastructure — a fast charger within roughly a 10-mile radius anywhere in Denmark — removes range anxiety; Jensen argues EV dissatisfaction elsewhere stems primarily from poor charging access.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Charging build-out is the gating factor for EV adoption in lagging markets.

insights.claim: From next year, Denmark will require all cars to be vehicle-to-grid ready; household-side V2G equipment is still being tested, and Jensen expects V2G to take off next year, calling the parked EV fleet Denmark's biggest battery.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Opportunity for bidirectional chargers and V2G aggregation platforms in Denmark.
insights.quote: the biggest battery you have in Denmark is what actually is parked right down here in the parking lot.

insights.claim: Declining fuel-tax revenue from EVs is reviving debate over per-mile road pricing (higher in cities with transit, lower in rural areas); trucks already pay it, and Jensen expects it for cars within some years.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Future per-mile charges could alter EV economics; watch for Danish road-pricing legislation.

insights.claim: Jensen says rising pension ages give Denmark fiscal room to manage lost fuel-tax revenue, contrasting it with Germany's pension-strained finances and a US with no fiscal room.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Fiscal capacity determines how gently governments can unwind EV subsidies and fuel taxes.

insights.claim: Jensen argues e-fuels and green hydrogen are necessary for aviation, long-haul shipping, steel and chemicals despite being less efficient than direct electrification, comparing their stage to EVs 15 years ago; about 80% of the world has never flown and demand will rise with incomes.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Long-dated Power-to-X demand thesis tied to aviation growth in emerging markets.

insights.claim: Denmark already produces green hydrogen for refineries, e-methanol for Maersk container ships and LEGO, e-ammonia for fertilizer and e-methane, and a German company just placed a multi-billion-kroner order for Danish e-SAF.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Commercial offtake for Danish Power-to-X is materializing; watch e-SAF offtake deals.

insights.claim: Denmark's large seabed area for offshore wind lets it produce more power than it consumes, positioning it to supply green hydrogen to German steel and chemical makers, since Germany has little seabed relative to land area.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Denmark–Germany hydrogen/e-fuel trade is a structural export theme.

insights.claim: A new Danish offshore wind farm powering about 1 million homes is coming online this year, and existing onshore wind/solar approvals and grid connections could double onshore output; Jensen says the constraint is now demand for green power, not supply.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: In Denmark demand creation (electrification) is now the binding constraint — favoring demand-side plays.

insights.claim: Jensen expects Denmark's cross-party climate consensus to hold because the center-right backs it on energy security and business case while the center-left backs it on climate, reinforced by a large wind-turbine export industry.
insights.speaker: Kristian Jensen (CEO, Green Power Denmark)
insights.so_what: Low political risk to Danish energy-transition policy relative to the US.
insights.quote: It is cheaper and better for our economy and our businesses to run on Danish produced power than on imported fuels.
